utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I can remind you, Admiral, of the affirmation that you took. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jokic, were your ships targeted by rockets wire guided from the top of the ramparts of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will now show you what you said in your interview to the investigators between the 1st and 5th of July, 2002, English page 154. You say: "My information was that there was shooting by rockets from the tops of the ramparts of the Old Town." The investigator said: "What sort of weapons were being used?" The answer was: "Rockets."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which kind of rockets?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guided rockets. It was either the Maljutkas or the German Armbrust. I'm not sure what the name was. There is such a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the target; land or sea?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target was the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How many rockets were fired on ships?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about details. I wasn't there in that battle yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would it be possible to provide the witness with the transcript if it is available, and also to give a time frame. The question was quite open.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe we discussed this last time: If my learned friend is stating that I am misquoting that particular transcript, please let her say so in order to avoid wasting any more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you assist me with the time frame of the question? Is that apparent or is the questioning not directed to any particular time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in relation to October, November, and December 1991, Your Honour. I believe the answer will indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Admiral --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not completed the quote since I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you had well and truly completed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the question of the investigator was: "How many rockets were fired on ships?" And the answer was: "Well, you're asking me about details. It wasn't yesterday that I was in that battle. I only know that there is a recording containing that information and I know that my ship was hit by a rocket. There were six people wounded, including the commander of the ship."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when did the rocket hit your ship?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, the operations around Dubrovnik were under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: October, November, or December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in November. And as I said, there is a recording which shows the exact position of the rocket that was being fired from the town walls. We can show the tape and we'll see about that. Mr. Jokic, is it true what you stated to the investigators in July 2002? Briefly, please. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking it's true, but I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please just tell me whether it's true or not, what you stated back in July 2002. Its's as simple as that. I do not need any further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... be allowed to answer, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The counsel is asking for an answer to his question. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you just please say whether it's true or not, what I just read out to you, that portion of your interview in July 2002.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not allowed to complete my answer about that rocket that hit the ship when there were six people who were wounded, and I wish to provide an explanation now. There was a later interview where I was given a chance to explain that. However, you're not quoting that one. I explained the position of the rocket, I explained the exact date, I explained exactly which the ship was in question, and I can repeat that for you if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No need for that, let's move on, please. Were there any ammunition warehouses inside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Not within the town walls, though. There was something to the east near the Ploce gate, near the Excelsior Hotel, perhaps 2 or 300 metres away from the Excelsior Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the truck-mounted weapon? Did it target your positions from Stradun? And Stradun, as we know, is within the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from our subordinate commanders from Zarkovica, Bosanka and Strincjera that there was such a weapon firing sporadic volleys, and then taking shelter immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In relation to this warehouse, there's something I want to ask you about as I have received my answer about the weapon. The English page is 160, the last line, and then continuing on 161, the investigator's question is, in July 2002 -- the investigator's question is: "Please let us clarify this. Regardless of the fact that you had received reports about your units on both land and sea coming under fire from the firing positions inside the Old Town itself, you still believed that the Old Town was a demilitarised zone, didn't you?" "A. Yes, I did, although there had been violations. They had weapons. They had a truck-mounted weapon which they used for firing from Stradun, which is in the centre of the Old Town and for firing in our positions. They also had an ammunition warehouse inside the Old Town just next to the Old Town harbour, and they're making no secret of that." Is it true that you stated that back in July 2002?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I said, next to the Old Town harbour, which is outside the walls, the Old Town walls. That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In November 1991, was the Old Town targeted? Did you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you have in mind is that we had received information or reports from subordinate commanders, no. We had no such official report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were the reports to the effect that firing positions outside the Old Town were being targeted?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, there may be an error in the transcript on line 15. The very first part of it I think counsel is reading and it has been quoted as an answer. Perhaps I can be corrected if wrong, but we heard it as a quote. I think it was from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quoting both the question and the answer from the interview. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. It has gone down as an answer in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript then appears to be misleading in that respect. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Your operations officer, Kozaric, did he at any time on the 6th of December order for the attack to be stopped? By conveying your own order, of course. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Kozaric authorised to convey such an order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. The Chief of Staff was not around, and he was the most senior officer at the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This order, would it have been sufficient for Kovacevic to stop it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. The commander was supposed to get back to me. He was not supposed to launch an attack. That was the fundamental thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said that at around 7.00 in the morning on the 6th of December you received a phone call from General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between 7.00 and 8.00 in the morning. I can't be sure about it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If at 4.45 in the morning you had been informed by Kozaric about the firing and the incidents in relation to the 3rd Battalion on the 6th of December, why, then, was the superior command not informed about that before 7.00?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 6.00, I received information that an attack had been launched by the commander of the 3rd Battalion and that there was one man dead and several men wounded. I was on the phone to Kozaric all the time, and I ordered him everything that needed to be done. The basic idea was to stop the attack being carried out by one of my subordinate commanders without proper authorisation. And wilfully, he wilfully launched some sort of an attack on Srdj. That was the fundamental thing for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said that at about 9.30 you received a second phone call from Minister Rudolf and he told you there was an attack under way against the Old Town and that he returned the receiver in such a way that you could hear the sound of shelling through the phone as you were talking to him and you believed what he was telling you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... counsel has misstated the time of the phone call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What do you say the time should be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My recollection from earlier evidence is about 8.30-ish, if the testimony is reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to adjust your question, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 4047, the times are given as stated by the witness. Therefore, my learned friend can go back to that record and verify that. This second call by Minister Rudolf came at 9.30, as has been stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you persist in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, even back then I said I wasn't sure about the exact time. I was on the phone in Cavtat. I was supposed to arrive there at 9.30. Then this might as well have been the exact time of the call. If I was talking from Kumbor, then it wouldn't have been possible for me to reach Cavtat by 9.30. Then we should probably put the conversation a bit earlier, but I wasn't sure even then, because I had at least two different phone calls with Minister Rudolf; the one we're referring to and another one much earlier when the minister claimed that the Old Town had come under attack, which I denied because I had not received any reports to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In this second conversation you had with Minister Rudolf, did you tell him that you would sort things out by 11:00 or, rather, that things would be sorted by 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say anything about sorting anything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that it takes two phone calls from Minister Rudolf for you to believe that the Old Town was under attack if as early as 7.00 you were told that you had to go and see the Federal Secretary for a briefing and that they had received calls from Dubrovnik in relation to the attack against the Old Town and that this had already been reported to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. It was on the basis of my conversation with General Strugar that I understood that, and General Kadijevic had told him that the town of Dubrovnik was being targeted. I wasn't sure, and I don't think it was said that the Old Town was in question. They just said the town of Dubrovnik generically, which would have been just as disastrous for us. During a cease-fire, there's a battalion launching an attack and targeting Dubrovnik. For me, that would have constituted sufficient reason to alarm everyone and try to stop the attack. I was not aware of the fact that it was the Old Town that it was being targeted. That was something that was for me to ascertain then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You issued an order to stop the attack at 11.00, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I issued one at 6.00 in the morning. Between 6.00 and 7.00 I was on the phone constantly to the command post at Kupari and to Brgat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard that already. So if you could please tell us what exactly happened at 11.00 as you remember it. Was there supposed to be a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At 11.00 Minister Rudolf called me and asked for an immediate cease-fire. I told him that some of my lines were down and that at 11.00 I would make an attempt to stop the attack. Yes, to stop any kind of attack at 11.00. That was the general meaning. We agreed on 11.00 although he has asserted 11.30. That's possible it may have been at 11.30, but what really happened is that the fire died down, subsided at 11.30 in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at 14.45 Kovacevic informed the command of the 9th VPS at the forward command post that he could no longer hold out at Srdj and that he had a number of different reasons to evacuate his men from there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14.45 I was not around, and this is the very first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was his attention drawn to the fact that he should evacuate people in an organised way and to mind the mortars and that it wasn't before 14.45 that the forward command post at Kupari approved Kovacevic's withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there at the time, but this is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that his withdrawal had not been approved prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's got nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Kovacevic need an approval to withdraw at all, given that he had never been ordered to attack in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it would not have been necessary. There had been no order in the first place, so it was all about Kovacevic. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is this a regular combat report of the command of the 9th VPS dated the 6th of December, drawn up by the Chief of Staff, Milan Zec?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should first be given a chance to just go through it briefly. I need some time to go through it and see exactly what it says in terms Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document was sent from the operations centre of the 9th VPS at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, if you look at item 1, passage 3, it says: "The enemy changed the positions of the mortars so fire was sporadically opened also from Stradun and from the area of the Old City port." Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading and that's indeed what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you could look at the last passage, the very last sentence. "Because of the impossibility to hold out at the position under such circumstances, pursuant to the request of the battalion commander of the 472nd Brigade, there was an approval from the forward command post to evacuate the unit from Srdj and bring it back into the earlier combat disposition, and this was done by 1700 hours." Does this, too, mean that he received approval to return to his previous position, an approval by the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the document states exactly when the cease-fire was ordered for.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the question because the speakers keep overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an approval from the Chief of Staff not to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you could look under item 4 on the next page. Item 4 on the next page, "Morale." The third sentence says: "At the same time, the success of the action in response to the long-lasting provocations from Srdj has positively influenced the morale of the units." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's your Chief of Staff. He's the one who wrote this, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to move this exhibit into evidence and may it please be assigned a number as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this document is D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me - you've seen this regular combat report now - why Kovacevic was not allowed to withdraw earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it says quite nicely in this report, and you omitted that, that at 700 hours he should stop action and stop the attack. You omitted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's go on. Was Kovacevic not allowed to withdraw earlier because it had been expected of him to succeed in keeping Srdj?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That has nothing to do with anything. This is actually contrary to the substance of the report that we've looked at just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that the command of the 9th VPS at 1540 on the 6th of December sent a message with the following content to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik? I quote: "Our forces have ceased fire in all parts of Dubrovnik at 12.45. We absolutely reject the possibility of having our forces operating at that given time, especially not against the Old Town. According to our information, the positions of Petka were hit from Kolocep, the command of the 9th VPS." INTERPRETER: The interpreters note that they don't have the text again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is counsel reading from so we can all orient ourselves and know what it is that's being referred to and being put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm reading from my notes, the questions that I made for this witness, and on the basis our investigator's investigations and the information that he obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you're giving the witness an opportunity to comment on what will be your evidence; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is precisely what my question is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He may be able to, or he may not. We will find out. And I take it further, just in case there's any doubt, that this is not presently the subject of any evidence before the Chamber. Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, I've read this message out to you. Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that message. Perhaps I was aware of it, but I wasn't there at the time; I was on that trip to Belgrade. But I can say one thing: As a soldier, I cannot accept, even in that situation, that it was possible from the island of Kolocep the other side was targeting the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was on Kolocep, which forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "their forces," you mean Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Through this message does the command of the 9th VPS say that the Croats are targeting their own forces, shooting at their own forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at 1605 Captain Stojadinovic informed the forward command post that because of the crossfire of the Croatian forces Petka, Lapad, Kolocep, the ship Rodos II could not sail into Dubrovnik? Is it an officer of the 9th VPS who is reporting about this internal conflict among the Croatian forces themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the Rodos ship incident. It had something to do with fire that was opened from land and from the islands, but I can't say what the nature of this fire was and who targeted who there. I remember it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how is it possible that through the forward command post in Kupari the artillery observers at Brgat and Zarkovica, with whom there was contact, that they did not inform you in Kupari about the attack on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't understand what you were saying. Whose attack on the Old Town; our forces or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: JNA forces, on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their observations were probably such that implied that artillery pieces were being targeted in order to neutralise their operation. It's not that the Old Town was targeted. That's not information that I got. Why would I get this information from them? I had my own Chief of Staff there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did the Chief of Staff not inform you that the Old Town was being hit, inter alia, or that shells were impacting on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've been saying he did not inform me while I was there that the Old Town was being targeted or, rather, that was his assessment perhaps, or perhaps there is some other reason, but I do not have any precise information that the Old Town was being targeted or that it was being shot at. I did not receive such information. But I did agree that shells were falling on the Old Town when I talked to Minister Rudolf, because I thought there was no reason for him to deceive me because it would soon be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You agreed, then, around 9.00 or 9.30 that morning, the 6th of December, that the Old Town was being hit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believed that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you not insist with your subordinates, because you had four colonels at positions near Captain Kovacevic, that the attack be stopped urgently and at all costs, the attack on the JNA operation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep forgetting that the link between Kupari and Zarkovica had been severed completely throughout the operations in town. Since I did not succeed in doing that, I issued an order from Brgat to have something done from Brgat, where the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion was, that the officer go to Zarkovica twice to stop the attack. That was at 12.00 and later on, I don't know exactly when, after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have contact with Brgat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kozarac could reach Brgat, yes. It was a weaker link, but it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how many metres is Brgat away from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Metres?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two or three kilometres. Certainly two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How much -- how far away is Kupari from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kupari to Zarkovica, as the crow flies, there is perhaps about six or seven kilometres; and by road, because it has to go via Brgat, it must be ten to 15 kilometres or ten to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you sure of this order of magnitude?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not but because since you keep asking me what the distances involved are I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about from Kupari to Cavtat by land?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Cavtat to Kupari, about 15 kilometres. It's much closer by sea, but by land it's about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how far away is it from Cavtat to Zarkovica, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To those 15 kilometres add those ten or 12 and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How much time does your vehicle need to cover that distance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why on the 6th of December from the morning when you were informed about the incidents and until 14.15 when you took off from Cilipi you did not come to your command post in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked to General Strugar and when everything that General Kadijevic had ordered was conveyed to me, I had told him about -- I actually told him what I was informed of from the forward command post in Kupari, and I said what I would do, and he agreed with that. That is to say that I was supposed to go to Cavtat. The negotiations were completed and the cease-fire was signed, and that was planned for 10.00, and at the same time the links with Dubrovnik that were rather weak from Kumbor or, rather, it took time to have it established, it was a direct link from Cavtat through civilian cables, and that was the main reason why I went to Cavtat. And then, as I waited for the helicopter that would come but the negotiations --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the transcript does not correctly reflect what the witness said. He is saying that negotiations had been scheduled on that day, the 10th of -- on that day at 10.00, and in line 21 that cannot be seen clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you not set aside half an hour on the 6th of December to go from Cavtat to Zarkovica and to personally stop the attack since you say you could not have found anyone through the communications system and if none of the people who you sent to Zarkovica was effective in stopping the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to look at the facts clearly and then judge. I sent my deputy, the Chief of Staff, to Zarkovica. Then Colonel Kovacevic, who I personally saw prior to my departure, and I even told him that he should replace the commander of the 3rd artillery battalion if he could not stop the attack in any other way. That is what I personally told him from the vehicle. I met him just on the outskirts of Cavtat. So I had my two most senior officers from my command there. And if the situation is unclear, according to our rules of combat, the commander should be at his command post, that he should not leave, and that was Kumbor. If I told General Strugar that I would be in Cavtat and hat we are not giving up on signing the cease-fire that had been scheduled for 10.00, and later on it was postponed until 12.00 and Rudolf agreed to that, that meant that I could not leave Cavtat before 12.00. Then the last thing: Why would a commander of my rank, a corps commander, go to Zarkovica where his deputy already was and also his assistant commander for the land forces? Would this ever happen that a commander of a corps commander rank and his deputy and his assistant go to one battalion in order to stop that kind of attack? It was not fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have any results in stopping the attack and having your order carried out? Were there any results in respect of that order of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the -- even at present when I look at the facts, when I look at them square in the eye, what I did was absolutely proper. To stop a battalion, if this was being done by officers, if they were carrying out my orders, if they were operating the way they were supposed to be operating, there would have been no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they operate the way they should have and did they carry out your orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all likelihood, they did not let the attack end, and the unit did not go back within the time realistically possible, about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that you did not see Kovacevic for seven or ten days. In respect to the 6th of December, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, this is an interview of Captain Kovacevic to the Politika daily newspaper. Are you familiar with the content of this interview?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This interview was conducted at Zarkovica, above Dubrovnik, on the 9th of December. You can see that by the journalist's report; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I see written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The witness has indicated no familiarity with this particular document. I don't know if there becomes any more relevance once he's said that, over the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you support what it is that you want to do with the document? It's not a document of the witness or of a conversation purporting to be with the witness, and he says he knows nothing about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to put questions to him in relation to the content of this document because I assume that he would have to know about some of these things, some of the information contained in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why don't you simply put those facts to him: Does he know about this or that or whatever they are. The document's just an unnecessary complication.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Savo Jovanovic, a TV cameraman from TV Montenegro who was in Dubrovnik with a group of JNA officers on the 8th of December when you sent that commission to record the damages incurred -- and this is referred to in the one-but-last paragraph of this article.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. I mean, I cannot remember all of that. Probably. His name is there if he was with that group of officers there on the 8th, but I cannot remember him just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have a press conference on the occasion of this particular event, the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you, at this press conference, say that the action on Srdj was not militarily justified but it has to be understood because this was a great burden on the officers and soldiers as human beings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said something to that effect because this was arbitrariness of a lower-ranking officer. His soldiers got killed, and he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wanted to revenge their deaths, and that things like that sometimes happen in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask this document -- for this document to be admitted into evidence and to assign a number to it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that will help you, Mr. Rodic. You have the admiral's indication that he did give or make a statement to the media which was along those lines. Isn't that what you want? You don't need the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but the substance of that is reflected in this document and that's why I moved that. But we can also have it merely marked for identification and just move on, because later on we will have another exhibit which has to do with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification because of time. At the moment I don't see why. Can it be given a Defence marked for identification number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document will be marked for identification as D63.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I'd like to distribute the following document. Your Honours, there is one thing I must explain in relation to this document. The fact is we do not have an English translation, but the document was obtained from the OTP during the cross-examination by the Defence. Therefore, we have not had sufficient time to obtain a translation, and I only have a very brief question in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is this a document of your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whose signature that is? There is a mark there. Is that you as the commander of the 9th VPS? Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think this is the Chief of Staff Zec's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a closer look.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It's not his either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could it be Kozaric's signature perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may this document please be given an exhibit number as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which Kosovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kozaric, the operations officers at the command of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, since we have no translation or understanding of where Defence is going with it, I'm not quite sure. We'll put this at the submission. And for re-examination, it would be a bit limiting unless we know where Defence is particularly highlighting its provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I've noticed it's merely a document apparently bearing a date in October and all that's said about it is that it's signed not by this witness even though it's over his printed name. I agree with you you couldn't do much with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be D64.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you talked to Captain Kovacevic about what happened around Dubrovnik in 1991 prior to your departure to The Hague in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell me why in your interview dated July 2002 you did not even mention to the -- you did not even mention the fact that on the 5th of December Kovacevic was in Trebinje, as allegedly he told you himself? Why did you not mention that to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention that. He really did tell me that, but I did not believe that was sufficient confirmation. He could frequently be unbalanced. I wasn't sure about the truthfulness of his statement once it was confirmed by officers from the command staff of the 2nd Operational Group, and when they told me about everything they talked about at the command post, it was then in 2002 or 2003 that I told the investigators about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I did not manage to track it down in the archive. I'm not sure where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a report on the action taken by the 3rd Battalion on Srdj on the 3rd of December, sent to the 1st administration of General Simonovic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript states 3rd of December, and it should be the 6th of December, not the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the document in the archive, the half-page report, less than a page, but I have never seen this one. In terms of how it looks, I would say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It's a detailed one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, detailed by all means, but I don't think it was there in the archive. It was never filed, which I found slightly surprising, because I had gone through the files. I checked. Was this done without me knowing about it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you see the stamp of the military archive, military files in the upper right corner?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that but I can't see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a document that belongs to your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of how it's made, how it looks, yes, but I didn't see this document in the archive, which means that I have not seen it for the last 14 years. Therefore, if I may just be allowed to -- to go through it, to have a look. Yes. Yes, in terms of substance it's all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please. Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Under item 1, the following information is provided in relation to Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, and the last sentence reads: "An exceptionally capable and brave officer." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You state the same in relation to Lieutenant Colonel Miroslav Jovanovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the one who wrote this, and I don't know this person. I think he only spent four days with me. Therefore, you should take this document only in very relative terms. I never met him, not even then and not up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you could look at item 4 of the document, the next page. The last bullet, the commander of the 3rd Battalion, Partisan Motorised Brigade removed from his position.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not the commander. Not the commander. He was a stand-in for the Commander Jovanovic. The commander was Srboljub Zdravkovic. He was a perfectly okay officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So where was Zdravkovic at the time? Did you allow him to leave the unit because of family problems?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had family problems and I allowed him, I authorised him to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you could look at item 5, the first portion: "Final and all-encompassing measures will be undertaken after investigation and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assessment of the overall situation."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there reference in this document to how the attack of the 3rd Battalion on Srdj on the 6th of December, 1991, came about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are the -- is the time line for the events on that day given?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to go through it and read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No. No need for that. Thank you. In the document, we can see that the command of the 9th VPS, the forward command post, as early as 6.50 in the morning, ordered the commander of the 3rd Battalion to cease operations of the 120-millimetre mortars but his unit was in such a position that this would only have caused further losses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. Whether it's true or not is a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It goes on to state that at 10.00 all commanders were again ordered to observe complete cease-fire, which our units did at 11.15; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And then it is stated that part of the forces of the 3rd Battalion remained on Srdj and they were under fire from the mortars of the National Guards Corps until 13.45 when it was decided that the unit should be evacuated from Srdj and sent back to its previous position. Who made this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was in charge, in command over there. But I do not think this --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So who was it who was in command there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about Chief of Staff Zec and Colonel Kovacevic, your assistant for land forces otherwise in charge of the 3rd Battalion on that day? Were they in command of this particular operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I established that once I was back and when I looked into this case, and I requested statements from them on what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the commander of the 3rd Battalion or, rather, the stand-in commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Miroslav Jovanovic, removed from his position on account of these events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this exhibit please be assigned an exhibit number as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The action report will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just another question in relation to this document since I didn't hear the answer. Is it true that this report was sent to the 1st administration, to General Simonovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the meeting you had in Belgrade with the Federal Defence Secretary on the 6th of December, you said that throughout the meeting, throughout the briefing with General Kadijevic, General Strugar remained silent.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Chief of Staff Blagoje Adzic and General Simonovic from the operations centre of the general staff, did those two attend that meeting? Chief of the operations centre; my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the 1st administration of the General Staff. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All of them, including yourself, remained silent while the Federal Secretary, General Kadijevic, was speaking, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. None of them spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: General Kadijevic, according to the rules of service, would address you in the formal way, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is nothing about that in the rules of service. You can't have rules for every single thing in the rules. He spoke to us as"Vi," he addressed us in the formal way, bearing in mind both myself and General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But did he also refer to General Adzic and General Simonovic when he spoke that way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never said anything to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this "Vi," this formal address, you distinguished yourself who that was a reference to, didn't you, who he meant by "Vi."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only telling you how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to JNA doctrine, is it customary for the Federal Secretary to criticise a superior officer in front of his subordinate officers, a superior officer in front of that superior officer's subordinates? Is that a customary way to go about it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doctrine doesn't say anything about. That's not what a doctrine is about. The doctrine is about the use of armed forces, about how --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, please. In practical terms, can you try to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the witness finished with his response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it was sufficiently indicated and it's been accepted and we're moving on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You, as a higher-ranking officer, as a commander, would you criticise a colonel who is superior to a captain in the presence of that captain? Just give me a yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In just any old situation, no, I wouldn't do that, but in a state of emergency, once the chips are down, you don't look at these conventional matters, at these military conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Kadijevic wanted you over for a briefing because on the 6th of December, 1991, all of this was happening within your area of responsibility, and your units were taking part in those things that were happening, units under your command? Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He called us to attend a briefing, not a report. He called the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, and he called me. We were the two people who were summoned. He didn't summon me because I was responsible for everything that was happening there. He called both my commander and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So why did he summon General Strugar, then, if General Strugar would have been perfectly able to explain everything himself? Or, rather, why didn't he leave you out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably assessed that General Strugar could not explain everything and that I need to be called too, but it is well known who was the most responsible in carrying out the Dubrovnik operation, because he gave orders to Strugar not to me. Not a single order during the operation was received by me from General Kadijevic or General Adzic. I never received a telegram from them, a dispatch, or did I ever talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you offer your resignation to General Kadijevic and did you propose to have Kovacevic removed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, what? Can you tell me exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me yes or no and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how is it possible that until you returned from Belgrade you did not know that the 3rd Battalion was in action, the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade? How come you didn't know about that until you returned from Belgrade on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on the basis of what I could have known that. Between me and this 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade there is a distance of about 30 kilometres or even more. Between us there are units and there is artillery, and they were operating all the time. And the firing of shells for 30 or 40 minutes from that battalion is something I could not hear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did the forward command post or your operations centre inform you about this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't know about it either. Only Zarkovica knew about that or, rather, the men at Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I would like to ask the usher, please, to distribute the following document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will have three or four minutes at the most on the tape, I think, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, isn't the first session until 3.45, for half an hour? That used to be the usual length until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Again you've caught me on the quarter hours, Mr. Rodic. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is this a report in the Politika daily newspaper dated the 9th of December, 1991, and does it have to do with the press conference that you held in Herceg-Novi on the 8th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the introduction, it says that on the 7th of December -- it says "yesterday," but since the press conference was held on the 8th of December, that means that on the 7th of the December on the ship Krila Dubrovnika, a cease-fire agreement was signed the sixteenth time. Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was. Maybe that's what written here but that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is not a cease-fire, it is an agreement. There were 16 cease-fires, but not a truce as such. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Look at the sub-heading "Fighting in Town." "Admiral Jokic especially pointed out that a huge fight occurred the day before yesterday in town itself between the members of the MUP and the ZNG on one side and the members of the HOS or Paraga's fighters on the other." Is that in accordance with the reports that I asked you about before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not deny that. I did not say that there was no fighting. I just said that there was no artillery fire. That's what I was suspicious about. As for firearms in town, I mean, that happened even in October, before that, the 29th, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The Croatian forces among themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this number please be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D66.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in this interview or, rather, I'm sorry, at the press conference, did you say that you found moral justification for what your battalion commander did on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. That was the expression I used. I had to find some justification when that unit had five dead and 14 wounded. What was supposed to be done was to minimise in a way or hush things up. That's the conclusion one would draw now. And even then, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why would you hush things up?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because such a big unit, a battalion, arbitrarily set out to attack despite all orders to the effect that this was not supposed to be done and because we were given such information about the damage in town and the casualties so that a person could not but feel affected by something like that. We thought that the JNA unit could not and should not do such a thing at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to put document P61 before the document, tab -- before the witness. 39, tab 39. That is the binder from Mr. Hvalkof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, we know you've been under pressure of time. What we propose is to break now to give you 20 minutes to collect your final thoughts and then give you the balance of the time then. I think that might be the best assistance to you rather than have you finish right now. So we will break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is this a report of your command or, rather, commission regarding the damages in the Old Part of Dubrovnik dated the 9th of December, 1991, that was sent to the Deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Stane Brovet?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why this document or, rather, the report on damage sustained by Dubrovnik is being sent to the deputy federal secretary?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Probably because he asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this document, is it correct that it was established in the one-but-last sentence that the origin of all the damages incurred cannot be established or the perpetrators named because obviously many were not caused by attacks from outside the Old City centre?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the conclusion of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you could not name the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appointed a commission that established the facts and gave its opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that opinion conveyed to you and were you made aware of the details that had to do with the findings of that commission?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: By your signature as commander and the most responsible person, do you stand by that opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appointed a commission that gave its opinion. That is its opinion. I was not asked to give my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, you said yourself that the deputy federal secretary asked for this kind of report from you. Is it correct that the deputy federal secretary did not appoint a commission consisting of these members of the command of the Military Naval Sector but that this was done by you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appointed the commission, and it wrote its opinion which is at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But this task has to do with you and your name, not this commission or any member of this commission. The federal secretary or, rather, the deputy federal secretary is giving you this task; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, aren't you wasting time over something that is crystal clear? It is the report which the admiral was required to prepare. He did not prepare it. He appointed others to prepare it. The report's contents are the work of those who prepared it, not the work of the witness. He forwarded it. They're the facts. It's not his opinion, but he accepted it and forwarded it. It was prepared by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the report that he sends to the federal secretary and that is the subject of my questions was compiled by the witness. He signed it, and he signed it as the most -- as the most responsible commander from the 9th VPS. The members of the commission did not send any kind of report to the deputy federal secretary with their own signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Rodic, why we're debating this. We do not disagree about the facts. I was pointing out to you that you seem to be going over the facts and losing time when you don't need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Actually, before introducing a new document, I would like to ask you whether this report addressed -- was addressed to Admiral Brovet just like the report dated the 7th of December that you sent to General Simonovic. Are they the result of the investigation that you carried out in the field upon orders from General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is part of that investigation that I had proposed to him. It's not that he ordered me. I proposed it to him and he agreed with that. He agreed, and General Strugar agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it already on the 6th of December, before you went to Belgrade, that you sent a letter to Minister Rudolf in Dubrovnik, stating to him that General Kadijevic asked for an energetic investigation to be carried out regarding the responsibility of the JNA with regard to the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what General Strugar conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are these the results of the energetic investigation ordered by General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is just part of it, to ascertain the damage in Dubrovnik. That is not the entire investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are the perpetrators referred to in these reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that this says is that the origin of all damages cannot be stated with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I asked about the perpetrators. In the report of the 9th of December and in the report of the 7th of December that you sent to Simonovic is reference made to the perpetrators who are responsible for the events of the 9th -- of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The perpetrators are not referred to, but it can be implicitly weighed, but explicitly there is no reference to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say then why the perpetrators were not referred to explicitly or the persons who were guilty for the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not have been mentioned because investigation had not been carried out. Statements had to be taken from all the responsible parties involved. This was only the very first crude material that was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you take statements from your officers who took part in these events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I conducted a hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly who you heard.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, Colonel Kovacevic, Colonel Jovanovic, Frigate Captain Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you conduct a hearing with regard to anyone from the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic before you removed him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a report as to when he opened fire, how many shells he used, against which targets. On that basis I informed General Strugar and asked for his urgent removal. I did not hear him, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During this testimony, why do you mention for the first time the report of the commander of the 3rd Battalion, that it was written, and that he was at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group when you said a few minutes ago that you did not hear anyone from the 3rd Battalion and also that you did not have any reports from them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that I had no reports. I said awhile ago that I did not hear them. The report did arrive, but not the one that we were shown, this two-page report here. Rather, there was a brief report that I found in the archive, hardly a page long, and this report states exactly what the 3rd Battalion did and why it launched an attack. We found this report at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Whose is this report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think its commander, but this should be easy to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the command of the 2nd Operational Group. That's where we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can the 3rd Battalion send a report to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... both implicated in this report and it would be very helpful to know about which is being spoken at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, good point, Ms. Somers. Could you make clear which 3rd Battalion, Mr. Rodic, and you have two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have in mind the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. That's the one I'm referring to. Is that the report that you had in mind, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the report of the commander of the 3rd Battalion. It is possible that it came through the operations centre in Kupari but I can't be sure now. It was found in the archive and it describes what the 3rd Battalion did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where do you have that document now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago that that was the document that I found in the archive and not the one I was given a minute ago. That's the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Are you in possession of that document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not, not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to have the transcripts of the following exhibit distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you've run out of questions and time, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we may just tender this into evidence. I'm perfectly aware of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a tape, a very short tape. It's not even a minute long, in relation to a press conference or, rather, the statement that Admiral Jokic made on the occasion in relation to the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Rodic. We'll have to call it a day. We've stretched and stretched to accommodate you. It is perhaps a great pity that much of this very significant material was not dealt with much earlier in the cross-examination when so much time was lost. That will have to be the end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to address you briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Rodic. We've had enough. Thank you. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we at least tender the interviews into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The ruling was no, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Admiral Jokic. I am going to ask you some questions that have arisen during the course of cross-examination, and I would like to start with something that's fresh before you. If I could ask that you be shown what was marked as Defence 62, please. It is D62. We could put D65 together if it would save steps for the usher as well. Admiral, I'm aware that because these were just put in front that the time of study them has perhaps not been very great, but I would like to ask you about the document D62, which purports to be a -- a report, a combat report of the day's events of 6 December 1991, purporting to be issued at 1700 hours. Was this after you had had your discussion with General Strugar about what you would tell the press as to the events of the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to be sure about that now, but I'm not sure which report you have in mind, the one to the 1st administration or the regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right now we're looking at the combat report that has --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- has Captain Zec's name on it. Was this done after General Strugar had indicated what version of the facts you were to accept, or the public?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe this one was made before then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you instruct Admiral Zec -- I'm sorry, Captain Zec at the time, to send this report, to compile and send it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the contents of the report before it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had no opportunity to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does -- do the contents of this report tend to agree with the version of the facts that you were instructed by General Strugar to accept? In other words, the Kovacevic version.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does this set of events as recounted in Zec's order reflect what you have described as a sense of regret that you communicated to Minister Rudolf not once but twice on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this doesn't reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does it reflect -- does this report reflect accurately the facts as you know them or really knew them to be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you agree with the contents of this report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with all the details. For the most part, I do agree. Naturally, there are a number of details that I do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May we take a look for a moment, Admiral, at D65. That is the other report which discusses various officers. Does this reflect accurately your own views and conclusions about the officers described here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Although it purports to bear your signature, or at least comes out under your name, were you in a position to put your own views of what actually happened on paper? Were you permitted to do so? In other words, were you free or did you find yourself under any pressure with regard to contents of these types of reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in no situation to be banned by my superior from writing such a report, but I was not able in such a brief time to verify every single detail in order to be able to draw up a report like this and send it off. That was up to the staff. Together with General Strugar, I accepted the view that, as it states here, the commander of the 3rd Battalion had been provoked into launching or, rather, provoked by firing from the Dubrovnik side to launch an attack on Srdj. I agreed with that, but I did not draw up a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the time, you agreed with that. Did there come a point where you learned that that was not accurate, not true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps several days later or thereabouts, when I wanted to carry out a proper investigation, that I realised that prior to launching the attack at 6 hours -- at 6.00, Captain Kovacevic had not suffered any casualties, and none of his soldiers had been wounded or killed. All of the dead and wounded were killed or wounded during the attack but not prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Look -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's what I found suspicious immediately, first thing in the morning at 6.00, when he did not even dare pick up the phone and speak to his own commander about the losses and casualties and perhaps to request an investigation. He failed to contact his commander for that whole day to seek advice on what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The document D65, in its entirety, if you look at it in its entirety, does it entirely reflect facts accurately?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not entirely. When they talk about acts of provocation by firing, there is a certain amount of exaggeration, and some facts are deliberately minimised.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could move on to D66, I believe it is, the press articles. And 63, if I could try to save some steps for Mr. Usher. Admiral, there are two news articles or two open source articles that were presented today to you, and my only question to you is: These come from the publication Politika; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1991, at the time of their issuance, can you please give us the orientation, the inclination, the tone, as it were, of Politika. What type of publication was it considered to be? What viewpoint did it represent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Politika was a newspaper playing up to the regime in power. They were among the warmongers very often. They were toeing the nationalist line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take a quick look at D66 under the rubric "Fight in the Town" which you were asked about on cross-examination. Did ever have information, as is suggested by Politika, that the forces on the 6th of December, the Croatian forces, were fighting among themselves? Is this something that you had heard about on the 6th of December? I'm focusing on that day in time, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Those clashes occurred on the 29th and 30th of October, and also, as far as I can remember, in November. However, in relation to the 6th of December, I don't know about that.
