I only know that after the 6th of December, the Orthodox church was damaged by an explosive that was placed at the threshold, but that has nothing to do with the fighting or anything that's stated in this article. However, as to the 6th of December and these clashes, I don't think we really had any such information, at least no reliable information to the effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So then as to this information that is contained about the so-called infighting, it is an inaccurate report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could call it unreliable. There were too many sources of information and too much information. It was only after a certain time that you learned the truth. I think this was one of the first things that came in from a source that was perhaps unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can we take a look, please, at D57. And I'd also like to ask if we could have a map - let's see now - given to you for your use. Looking at, first of all, D51 -- I'm sorry, 57, excuse me. There's a reference in the first paragraph. There's a reference to the use of an 82-millimetre and a 60-millimetre gun. It says "from the fortresses of the Old Town." Can you please, first and foremost, explain what the fortresses of the Old Town were.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were the fortresses at the corners or edges of the town ramparts, at each of the corners; you had altogether four such fortresses. Specifically, Bokar, St. John's, Minceta, and Revelin. Those are the four names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you in a moment to try and point them out, but as you refer to these as fortresses, were they situated within the walls of the Old Town or are you making a reference to the turrets, the turrets of the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are towers with turrets. They have an entrance and an exit inside the walls, the body of the walls. Therefore, they're half inside the town, in a manner of speaking, and half outside, facing outside, at least. Their function was to defend from outside attacks when they were built back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have mentioned sheltering behind the walls and behind the fortresses during the course of cross-examination. Did you intend to mean within the walls or outside the walls when you discussed sheltering of perhaps weapons? If you give me just a second, I'll give you -- I'll try and get the wording that you used. You had indicated that there were weapons sheltered behind the walls, behind the fortresses. Did you have in mind outside the walls?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does this response that you've just given about outside the walls also apply to the reference of fire being opened from the fortress in the Old Town by a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second. Then just to make sure it's clear, the weapons that were referred to were outside the Old Town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is extremely inappropriate the way in which my learned friend and colleague is asking her questions. He's talking about a fortress, a fortress. It's a concept which should be clear to everyone what is a fortress, what is the Old Town. We've talked about that dozens of time in this courtroom, and let my learned friend and colleague is persistent in trying to somehow twist the meaning into having this fortress that is around the Old Town, that is part of the Old Town centre somewhere outside the Old Town. So please can we try to be fundamentally accurate about the geography of the Old Town. This fortress is simply an integral part of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's perfectly correct, Mr. Petrovic, but what Ms. Somers is asking about is the evidence of the witness when he spoke in particular about forces sheltering by the walls or into the walls or sheltering behind the walls of the fortress, and what's essentially being cleared up is whether that meant they were inside the fortress or outside the fortress. I think that's a useful and correct approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one sentence. What my learned friend and colleague is taking as her departure point is the sentence that reads: "From the fortress of the Old Town centre." That's where she starts out from when providing document D57. That's the point of departure, from the fortress of the Old Town centre. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, when I ask you, please, when we discussed the 120-millimetre mortars that you just explained that you had in mind were outside the Old Town, what was the time frame? Can you tell us when this would have applied during the period? During what period would it have applied?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have applied to the period starting with the beginning of October and on when the units under my command arrived in the Zarkovica area, and prior to that, until the 26th or 27th of October, I don't know exactly. I was in no position to be receiving reports nor were my units in the area, therefore, my statement relates to the period of time after the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the document D57 that you have, can you please look at the document and indicate whether or not there is any reference to mobile mortars being used by the -- what is described as "the enemy" in the document. I ask you this because Defence counsel had put to you the use of mobile mortar units. Can you indicate if that is in fact in that document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I believe I provided a very detailed description of that the last time around. There are for me no mobile mortar units --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm asking you if in the document itself there is a reference to mobile mortars.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the paragraph under 1, "From the fortresses of the Old Town centre, the enemy is using mobile mortars, 82- and 60-millimetre ones." I said back then that this wasn't possible, to use mortars to fire from the Old Town walls in view of the concrete surface in which these mortars would have been positioned. This would not have been possible. It was possible for them to be placed adjacent to the walls, near the turrets where there was sufficient shelter from behind which they could operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. I was just waiting for the translation to finish. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may point out an error in the interpretation. There is something missing. From the walls of the Old Town centre they were using mobile, mobile ones. Unfortunately, that's missing from the transcript. [Previous translation continues]... "[In English] using MB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's on page 55, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes. By your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you're saying it's missing from the translation of the document, not from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll explain now. It's not in the transcript because it's not in the written document. That is the situation we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, when you referred, page 55, line 13, placed adjacent -- we're talking about, this would not have been possible. "It was possible for them to be placed adjacent to the walls near the turrets." Are you referring to outside, again outside the walls?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look on -- I hope the map you have is adequate. If the ELMO is able to depict the area of the Old Town or at least allow the admiral to look at the area of the Old Town. Are you able to see -- could you identify, please, Admiral Jokic, the area on this particular map which would identify the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this Exhibit D57?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is not. This is a map that we have just put in front of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a different and new map, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have moved away from an inquiry on D57, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Admiral. I was looking up at Judge Parker. Could you do that again, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So the Old Town area, if you could just show its overall area.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to identify the positions outside the walls where the alleged 82-millimetre and 60-millimetre guns referred to in D57, as we just talked about, or 120-millimetre weapons, referred to in another exhibit, D51, may have been? And if you can, could you mark, please, as you understand the locations. I just want to -- before I have you mark, I need to check the colour for the Prosecution. With a blue marker, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Objection, Your Honours. Perhaps the witness is in a position to say something about some other 60 and 82-millimetre mortars but certainly not these from document D57, because what it says here is from the walls of the Old Town. Therefore my learned friend and colleague may also choose a different question, but if she's asking a question in relation to this document, that's certainly not what we're talking about. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the witness had answered what his intention was when he answered that question; we're discussing outside the walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got all of us confused, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness said of D57 that he meant outside the walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But he also then went on to say that there was a reference to the enemy using mobile mortars from positions in the turrets of the Old Town, and he added his observation that that was simply not possible because mortars could not be fired from those positions because of the nature of the surface on which a mortar would be placed. They need to be on earth, if I recall his evidence, not on a surface such as stone. So we've got --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I mean to confine my question to the areas outside the walls, outside the walls where mortar units you have discussed may have been placed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I point this out? It is here where it says this part, "Pile," park. That's where the 120-millimetre mortars are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there a particular name that you associate with the park?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's Pile, the Pile park. That's the area of the Old City hospital. That's where the Old City hospital is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there a -- have you heard of a reference to a place called Bogisica park?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a different park on the other side. I don't see it here, though. Or maybe I made a mistake, but I think it's on this side. I didn't have this map before, so... On this other map it says Bogisica park, so it would not have been confusing in any way, but this is a new map that I haven't seen before. That park is not marked on this map. The colour map, that's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, Admiral, whether or not that is the 120-millimetre mortar group that may have been referred to in one of the documents, like probably D51?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is one or two mortars of 120-millimetres. That was also confirmed by witnesses and some other sources, some intelligence sources. As for the exact time when they fired, I cannot say for the 120-millimetre one. As for the 82-millimetre one from Bogisica park, the situation is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to, if you can from this map and I realise you say you haven't seen this particular map before, indicate the positions of the alleged 82- and 60-millimetre weapons? Again, only if you can from this map. These are the ones that Defence counsel placed on D57 in their exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's approximately these positions, 82 millimetres in Bogisica park, four artillery pieces that fired the most on the 6th of December, and all the time they were firing at Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you give us, if you are able --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here at the Srdj feature it says 412 metres. That's the altitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask you another question, if I could, please. The distance from the locations of the mortars, if you can, to the Old Town first, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for 82-millimetre mortars, the distance is 200 to 300 metres. As for 120-millimetre ones, the distance is somewhat longer; 300 to 400 metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Are you able to indicate Lokrum island? Lokrum island? I'm going to ask if you can indicate several locations on this map.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The island of Lokrum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And can you indicate also, please, the Belvedere Hotel. If you -- if you'd like to, before you leave Lokrum --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Before you leave Lokrum, if you'd just mark it with an 'L' with your marker so we know that's what you've identified, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now moving on, if you could show us where the Belvedere Hotel is, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to move the map over so that we can -- yeah. Good. All right. The 'B' is for Belvedere, Admiral; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Hotel Libertas.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you could mark it 'HL' for Hotel Libertas. Make it a little -- because you've used that initial already. Just 'HL.'

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Argentina.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's the 'A.' And the Excelsior.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 'E.' And Cape Petka.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You've marked that with 'RP'; is that correct, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you -- if you're able to see it on that map, could you indicate where the Kolocep island is, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map it cannot be seen. It is outside this map, but it's on this side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll try perhaps -- we appreciate that. We'll try another map later that will have it. Can you give the distance of Kolocep island from the Old Town of Dubrovnik -- or to the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long distance. I can't estimate it. You should have a look at the map and then it is quite clear that I cannot estimate the distance between the port of Gruz and Kolocep. It's over ten or 12 miles; that is to say over 15 kilometres. Then from the port of Gruz to the Old Town there is another six or seven kilometres. It's a long distance. It's over 20 kilometres, maybe even 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is that -- is the distance why you indicated it was improbable that fire in Kolocep would have been directed against the Old Town and caused damage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is physically impossible to target something like that. It would be hard to expect anyone to fire at the Old Town from Kolocep and to actually hit it, because there are many artillery pieces in town if anybody wanted to target it at much closer range.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, are you able to give the scale of the map that you're looking at, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1:5000, I think. It's not even a real map. It's a plan map. It is like a town map, not a real, proper map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In -- in cross-examination, Admiral, you were asked and you indicated markings for the suspected 120-millimetre position between the Argentina and Excelsior Hotel. I think you said on the Ploce gate side. Are you able, first of all, to indicate in what time period you had that in mind; and if you could indicate on this map.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here. The warehouse that was referred to was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you mark it --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says "Ploce," that is where the ammunition depot was. We thought it was there, in the area of Ploce. And the mortar, according to some reports, was here, in this area, and we did not know whether it was 120-millimetres or 82-millimetres, but for a while it operated from here. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could I ask, just for the record, Admiral, you have an 'S' for where you indicated the warehouse, is that correct, an 'S,' the letter, and then an 'M' for mortar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated what you indicated was an ammunition warehouse. Is that correct, Admiral? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximate distance between what you have marked as 'S' to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 200 metres, 250.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And 'M,' what you have marked as 'M,' the distance from 'M' to the Old Town, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Other than the positions that you have marked, did you have any information of any Croatian military positions within close proximity to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At what time is this, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Between the 7th of October when the admiral took over, 7th, 8th of October and the 31st of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, Admiral? If not, I will repeat it for you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is your answer then, please? Did you have any other information of any Croatian military positions within close proximity to the Old Town in that time period other than the positions that you have marked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from these positions, of course I followed intelligence reports which came down the chain of command from the 2nd Operational Group during the month of October, although I was not in a position to see this and confirm it until we came to the town itself or, rather, Zarkovica. We had information that in the month of October, and even at the beginning of November, from the positions of the walls and turrets there was firing coming from small arms and sniper fire, too, and there was even one particular piece of information that defenders were noticed who had a rocket launcher as well. In order to be as objective as possible, this information was often corroborated, sometimes reliably and sometimes unreliably, but the fact was that there had been gunfire from small arms coming from the walls. There was no firing of rockets, but a rocket launcher operator was seen. Later on during the month of November, probably when the UNESCO mission came, on the walls defenders could no longer be seen with weapons or was there any such fire coming from the old walls. So in addition to the positions I pointed out, that is what was written in our intelligence reports and what was noticed from features and positions close to town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The information, then, you're referring to only goes up to approximately early November, as I understand what you've said. On the 6th of December --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. As far as I could see, in 64, it says: "Later on during the month of November, probably when the UNESCO mission came..." That is page 64, line 8. What we have here is knowledge about what was going on in November and also when the mission came in November. So it certainly cannot be put the way my colleague put it, putting the question in an inappropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to try to give the time frame, then, as to when you no longer believed it was the applicable situation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot link myself to any date, but following the operations of the other side and on the basis of our observations and reports, I can only see such a sequence of events. If I want to be quite frank and quite truthful, that is the only thing I can say. I cannot link myself to any particular date. What happened in October and the beginning of November, perhaps up to the middle of November, I don't know. There were such things observed, but later on there weren't. Because I do not know the exact date when the representatives of UNESCO came and whether this had to do with them at all, but I'm just assuming.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let us -- let us then ask -- let me ask about the 6th of December. Was this situation the situation as you may have been informed on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 6th of December we did not have any such observations, namely that on the walls or within the Old Town there were operations or, rather, that there were weapons except for what I marked a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking back for a moment at D57 - do you still have it in front of you? I'll try to finish all references so we don't have to go back and forth to it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at paragraph -- I believe it is 5.4, there is the passage in the middle where it says: "Discover the combat enemy positions and they should be destroyed in the region," et cetera, et cetera, "and report on enemy positions and be mindful not to act on the Old Town." Do you see that, Admiral? It starts out saying, "Discover combat enemy positions --"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And at the end it says, "while being mindful not to act on the Old Town." Now, does this indicate that any discovery should be reported to the command and that there is no fire to be permitted at such positions first, even if discovered?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports of such discovery pursuant to this order from your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, apart from what I drew on the map and what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You have indicated that your subordinate officers on vessels had reported to you that they had been fired at and that they had fired at positions in the vicinity of the Old Town. I'm talking vessels, Admiral. Do you know what those positions were? Were they the same positions that you had already marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all these positions that are marked on the map, including the positions on the islands. It's not mentioned here, but on the island of Lokrum there was a 20-millimetre cannon on the top of this hill, where this 'L' is. Then also on the island of Kolocep there was a 20-millimetre or 40-millimetre gun. And on the island of Sipan, there were cannons of 85 and 88 millimetres. However, that's far away from the town of Dubrovnik. That's where they had rocket positions, too, Maljutkas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you had stated that they had reported to you that they had fired at hotels in the vicinity of the Old Town. What were these hotels? Were they the same ones you have indicated on the map you just marked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's those hotels: Belvedere, Argentina, Excelsior, Libertas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked during cross-examination about the firing rockets, I believe. Rockets being fired from the walls of the Old Town. You started to give an answer and you were interrupted. Are you able to complete the answer? It was a reference, I believe, from one of the interviews. Could you please complete what you started to say.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Patrol boat 137 on the patrol line in the Kolocep channel on the 20th of November was attacked by two rockets, 9K11 Maljutka, of which one hit the command bridge and wounded the commander and five sailors as well. That was in the area and light -- of the island and the lighthouse of Olip, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you do it as quickly as possible, in the interests of time, if you could explain your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's over 30 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the interview as was referred, was the reference to firing from the Old Town correct? The walls -- excuse me, the walls of the Old Town, if I remember correctly, is what was cited. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was said, but I didn't manage to finish my answer as far as the rocket fire was concerned. It was that rocket fire that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Admiral. You had made reference during cross-examination to an ammunition warehouse outside the Old Town in the harbour area, I think you said near Ploce -- near Ploce or near the Excelsior. Is that the same ammunition warehouse you had marked on the map just a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had indicated that despite orders from the 2nd Operational Group to take the facility in Srdj, you did not allow it to be taken. Can you explain why not and what your concern was. Will you be referring to the map, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought, but... On the map Srdj can be seen quite clearly. Trig point 412, which constitutes the central bastion on which the defence of the town was based. The Defence line goes from Srdj to the Belvedere Hotel and to Nuncijata. When Srdj would fall, which has this enormous so-called Imperijal fort and also an underground tunnel that goes to town, if that feature were to fall, the defence of town would fall too. When an attacker would take that particular feature, then there would be no obstacles on his path in terms of entering the Old Town. The Old Town is, from Srdj, is not more than 600 metres away from Srdj as the crow flies. So it would have been a catastrophe for any ordinary soldier let alone commander to take -- to have that feature taken, especially in a situation when around the town in a blockade there is a brigade plus a few battalions. That's about 10.000 men. Who would be in a position to exercise any kind of control in terms of this battalion that would take the fortress? Who would ever stop them from entering town as well? On the 8th of November, we had a particular case when Bosanka was taken and when a group of about 20 soldiers came of their own free will to Srdj, and they suffered losses there. Of course not only because of that case but because of the importance of the feature of Srdj and our intention and objective of the 2nd Operational Group not to take the town and not to fire at the Old Town. I think that my primary duty was to prevent the taking of that particular feature, and at the same time to make it impossible in terms of that facility that was the most heavily armed and heavily fortified to prevent any kind of fire to come from there vis-a-vis our units and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask that the witness be allowed to finished this answer because he was stopped in half-sentence in terms of what were the things that were supposed to be done according to his own idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think the witness has given the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there more you wanted to say, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May I, just a minute? So the objective was to disable any fire coming from that feature, to use fire to destroy the weapons that were firing at our front end. We succeeded in doing that. On the 11th or 12th, because of major losses suffered, Srdj will be abandoned [as interpreted]. However, we did not take it although it had been abandoned. And when the defenders saw after three days that we were not entering Srdj, they went back. That is the real truth about the feature of Srdj, which was the key of the defence of Dubrovnik and a lure for our units. And one particular commander on his own bat tried to take revenge for his own losses and therefore wanted to take Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What I wanted to get a response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm just going to call a halt now. I think we've had more than an answer to your question, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will have the break now and then if there's any further question you want to put, you can. Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- something?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in relation to the interpretation. Page 69, line 18, it says "Srdj will be abandoned." What the witness said is that "Srdj had been abandoned." So the forces under his command did not take Srdj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We will have the break now and then see if there's more needed on this topic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to tender the map into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked P146.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, we are under a tremendous time pressure, as you can appreciate, so I'm going to ask you to answer briefly my questions and even where there are exhibits we'll try to move very quickly. If I can ask you to please have a look at a document that will be passed out by the usher imminently. While we're distributing the document, I'm going to ask you, Admiral, Defence used a number of reports prepared by the assistant commander for morale, political and moral affairs, as sources to describe the situation in the zone of operations. I'm going to ask you just very briefly to provide an overview of the activities of the assistant commander for political and moral affairs, looking at the document in front of you which is the rules, basically, on the -- it's the 1990 corps peacetime report. If you would turn in English, please, to what is page 1. It ends in ERN 0014. And, Admiral, for you it would be in the B/C/S, it ends -- up above in the right-hand corner it says 01147081. It has the number page 23 at the top. Perhaps if the usher is in a position to -- it starts at 01147080 in the B/C/S. You don't have to worry about going through the whole list. I'm going to ask you a very quick question about it, but -- yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can only say, Ms. Somers, that the numbers you gave do not coincide with the numbers we have, but I don't -- just so that the record reflects that. We have the document and you cannot delay about sorting out the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What I'm asking you to turn your attention to, Your Honours is the organ for political work and -- sorry. Organ for political work and legal affairs. That's the rubric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you about the propaganda aspect involved in this position. If you look at paragraph 20 -- or point 20, excuse me, under the general title of Assistant Commander for Political Work and Legal Affairs, Article 21, there are a number of points. The reference is to the studying political and propaganda work in the armed forces of potential aggressors and proposing and taking necessary steps. Is a propaganda element part of the job of moral -- or political and moral officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We're not talking about propaganda here. This is about political activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But is propaganda, and not necessarily in a bad sense, but propaganda meaning an objective attached to a particular type of speech, is that part of the job of a political and moral officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask that it be received into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not objecting to having this document tendered into evidence but as this is a new document, we would like to have at least three or four minutes to cross-examine the witness in relation to this document since this is the very first time that we see this document. Therefore, we are adamant that we should be given a chance to ask a couple of questions in relation to this new document. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Petrovic, the answer is no. The document is put in in response to detailed cross-examinations based upon the work of the officer of this description, and the document is tendered merely to give some indication of the role of that officer. You may, in final submission, if you wish, draw upon its content, but not to cross-examine. Carry on, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can you explain to the Chamber, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we haven't yet got the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I got ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number for this document is P147.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can we move on to another topic, please. Can you please explain how you were able to determine which unit of the 2nd Operational Group was responsible for shelling the Old Town in November 1991? Now, you did not receive reports from subordinate units, but how -- how did you determine what units were responsible? Again, please, as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't exactly determine which units, but I said which the units were that were objectively in a position to target the Old Town, which is the artillery of the 472nd Brigade, and the 3rd Battalion of that same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And for December 1991, for the 6th of December shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 6th of December, it could only have been the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You indicated you had not received reports from subordinate units on these incidents. Despite the absence of reporting, did you learn that the Old Town had been shelled in November of 1991, even though you did not receive reports from units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following those operations, based on direct reports, or, rather, indirect reports through the media and secondary sources of information from the accounts of refugees, we learned that damage had been caused to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Moving on, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the impact was of the creation of the 2nd Operational Group on the territorial borders which you drew on maps D41 and D42. If you need to see these, I can quickly put them to you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you understand the question then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. If I understand your question correctly, it's about the task or, rather, what the objective was surrounding the setting up of the 2nd Operational Group. Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, the question has to do with the territorial borders, the impact of creating the 2nd Operational Group on the territorial borders which you drew on those two maps. Were the boundaries that you had drawn on those two maps still relevant once the 2nd Operational Group came into existence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boundaries drawn there, you mean the republican boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which boundaries you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Hold on. We'll show you very quickly the documents. D41 and D42. Do you have them in front of you? And you can take a look at them quickly, Admiral. You showed certain boundaries. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Those are the boundaries between military districts --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I don't know them by heart, but I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't see the ELMO. We can't see what's on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you see them, Admiral? Okay. Did those boundaries, did the boundaries that are drawn have an impact on the operations of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly describe the impact.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the existing boundaries, the way the armed forces were structured and organised in the then-JNA, the objective that had been set could not be carried out without setting up a new command that would unite all the operations or coordinate all the operations in this area under the existing boundaries of the various military districts shown on this map. The task could not be carried out. So-called Dubrovnik Operation could not be carried out. A new command had to be set up with new units that would carry out the task and obtain the objective of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So these boundaries were not relevant to the operations of a 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you quickly a couple of questions of -- first of all, sorry, let me just ask you this: What was General Jeremic's formation, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 2nd Corps, of the Podgorica Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And to which formation was the 2nd Corps subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we should have a time frame for this. May my learned friend and colleague please ask about the specific time frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the commander of the 2nd Corps. He had been prior to the Dubrovnik operation also. The establishment was it was a command that was resubordinated to the 2nd Operational Group the moment it was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From 1 October through 31 December, was that the situation that prevailed? Is that yes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Admiral, are you familiar with the 1984 rules of service of the security organs in the armed forces of the SFRY as well as are you familiar with the 1985 service regulations of the SFRY armed forces military police? These are two different bodies of regulation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to distribute simultaneously these two documents. If I can ask you if you have in front of you the document that would be labelled -- that would be called Rules of Service of the Security Organs of the Armed Services. Can you please take a look at Article 16 as well as 17. 16 is the principal one. Yes. This is the 1984 publication, Your Honours. From the provision that says, "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command, unit, institution or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed in the establishment and it is responsible to that officer for its work while JNA security organs in organisations for NVO are responsible to the competent Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence." Are you familiar with this provision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a well-known provision. Every officer knows it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, but could we be informed what "NVO" is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, would you be kind enough to explain the abbreviation "NVO."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This NVO organisation, armament and military equipment. These are semi-military organisations in charge of armament and military equipment. These are actually military factories, and they're under the Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence. They have a slightly different structure. These are no combat units, these are military factories.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving quickly on to the second document in front of you. I would ask you to turn your attention, please. This is the document on the military police. If you could look at paragraph -- or Article 12, paragraph 12, please. The provision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't yet got the number of that last document, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- I'm sorry, the ERN, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, no. The exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Should I do it one by one? I was going to try to move them together but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood you had moved them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm in such a hurry I'm ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're receiving the one dealing with the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which will be Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 148, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P148. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: MS. SOMERS: Sorry, Admiral, for confusing you. The second document I'd ask you to look at, Article 12. The familiarity with the provision, "The officer in charge of the military unit, an institution within whose establishment the military police unit is placed or to which it is attached commands and controls the military police." Are you familiar with this? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask to move this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As my learned friend and colleague is introducing documents that have to do with military regulations and it is very important that in addition to Article 12 the witness also explain Article 13, which is directly related to it, because there is a separation in relation to the command and control over military police, and I believe the witness is in a position to explain what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't think it's relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've drawn the witness's attention to 13 -- to 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you're asking for comment or explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just an acknowledgement of familiarity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, based on JNA doctrine, would this mean, looking at this provision, 12, would this mean that General Strugar was authorised to task the security organs and the military police of the 2nd Operational Group to investigate alleged violations of the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what my learned friend and colleague claims is simply not in evidence. During the examination-in-chief, the witness said that the 2nd Operational Group had no other kind of military police except for the military police that was attached to the command, and that's the only thing that the witness stated in order to provide security for the command, for headquarters, nothing else. And there's no other role that the witness attributed to this military police during the examination-in-chief. Therefore, what my learned friend is insinuating now is nothing that the examination-in-chief seems to indicate, or the cross-examination for that matter. If you would please have a look at what she's implying by asking this kind of question. Can we please have a question stated in a fair manner and say exactly loud and clear what it's in relation to and what it's supposed to clarify. When was this ever referred to during our cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the question does arise out of cross-examination, Mr. Petrovic, and the question posed is whether by virtue of 12 of chapter 2 it was within the competence of General Strugar as the officer in charge of 2 Operational Group to task military police of that group to do certain things. And the answer is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this article, by your leave, Article 13, just under Article 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Article 12 is sufficiently clear. The military police are subordinated to the commander of the unit of which it is part, and the same goes for the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And we would like to put it in evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, what is this continual one alternately with the other interrupting that's going on? There is a very tight time frame. If you have a serious objection, you may raise it, but this was a clear question arising out of your cross-examination. We have noted that you want us also to take note of Article 13, and we will do so, but it's up to Ms. Somers whether or not she wishes to ask about Article 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say something in relation to the cross-examination. During the cross-examination and also during the examination-in-chief, the witness indicated that the command of the 2nd Operational Group only had one platoon, one police platoon to provide security for the building of the command itself, and there is a huge difference between that and what is being asked now in terms of these military regulations. I think the witness is well placed to explain that and that's why I wanted to speak about it, because the military police has a clear structure and the witness indicated exactly which structure of the military police General Strugar had inside the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers. If you'd carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think my last request was to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked as P149.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't think you have in front of you but I'm going to ask to have placed quickly in front of you a -- the All People's Defence law, an excerpt from it. While it's being -- while this document is being distributed, Admiral, I'm going to ask you -- well, I think it probably makes more sense to wait until you've seen it. If you could look, please, at what is an excerpt of the 1982 Law on All People's Defence and turn your attention to Article 93, Article 93. Are you familiar with this provision, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The provision obliges at all times and in all circumstances abiding by international laws of war. Does a lack of sufficient number of military courts relieve a commander of his obligation to maintain and restore military discipline including the obligation to act against alleged violations of the laws of war? And I take -- ask you to look at it in the context that I have just raised.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this Article is unambiguous in providing always and under all circumstances for this, irrespective of whether there is enough military police or military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I would ask to please move the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P150.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you had referred during your examination to certain difficulties communicated to you by the military prosecutor in Split. Are you aware of any request that has been submitted either by your command or the command of the 2nd Operational Group requesting adequate staff and officers for the military court from the relevant organs of the JNA? Just a yes or no, please, because of time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't submit anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to distribute, please, rather quickly, another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What you have in front of you is a document proclaiming existence of imminent war danger in the SFRY. Are you familiar generally with this -- this provision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You stated in your testimony that although a state of war had not been declared, the factual situation on the ground was that of a war. As such, although a state or a declaration of state of war had not been made, the environment, the time was also not considered peacetime either?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I please move this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to have two different documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to have two different documents distributed to the Chamber. I have two pages, one in English and one in B/C/S. Judge Thelin has a much larger document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, there should be one in B/C/S and then effectively three pages attached in English. Is there -- was that misdistributed perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've now been given one the same as the other two members of the Chamber, which is the one you apparently intended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the Chamber has a chance to glance at it, does it show Belgrade 1 October 1991, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the problem on the second page - in the English translation it's the first page - is that it's speaking of a Gazette of 18th of October 1991, speaking, if one goes to the last paragraph above the heading Proclaimed Existence of Imminent War Danger, it's speaking of a session held on the 1st of November and yet gazetted on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We could ask the admiral to explain why the differences in the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, do you still have the document in front of you? The question, Admiral, is the actual existence of imminent war danger in the SFRY has a date of 1 October 1991, which you can see in B/C/S where Dr. Kostic's name appears, but that the overall document in which it is contained, the Sluzbeni List, has a date of 18 October, 1991. Are you able to explain why the different dates occur? Is there something in the administrative code? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have found the answer to our problem. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Admiral. It's a mistranslation. If one goes to the B/C/S, the date there is 1st of October, not 1st of November. So we'll make that alteration and you needn't trouble the admiral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral, for your willingness. Admiral, along this theme, however, in addressing the Defence question on the issue of the difference in the regimes of law and regulations applicable when there is a state of war as opposed to peacetime, you went on to say that the law provided that during a state of war, small misdemeanors and offences which would otherwise be punishable during peacetime go unpunished because military courts have to concentrate on actual crimes. First, can you give us what is your understanding of misdemeanors or offences, with possibly an illustration, as quickly as you can given the time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said the following: That disciplinary infractions -- I did not say misdemeanors; I said infractions or offences, minor ones, are not investigated and punished in a state of war, and that is what is written in a particular set of rules. Probably because there is not enough time. There is no possibility to do that. It is only for crimes that people are held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you give an example of an infraction, something you had in mind as an infraction.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if two soldiers fight or if a soldier gets drunk but does not commit a particular offence or cause any damage, that would be sanctioned in peace but not in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would shelling a protected civilian object, such as structure or structures in the Old Town, be considered as an actual crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a legal question for the Honourable Trial Chamber. I do not see how the witness is going to respond to this question. I kindly ask that such questions do not be put to the witness. All similar questions that the Defence wished to put with regard to this subject were objected to by my colleague and were therefore rendered impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is something in the commander's determination as a command decision, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're asking not the question you asked in so many words but whether as a commander he would treat the shelling as of this nature, you may ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Putting the question in the command framework, as a commander, would you consider shelling a protected civilian object, such as one in the Old Town of Dubrovnik, would you consider it as an actual crime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, is it an actual crime immaterial, irrespective of whether or not it is a peacetime or state of war or imminent threat of war? Does that make any difference or does it remain an actual crime that is punishable at the time? Excuse me. I'll make sure I've got the question as I have drafted. Hold on a second. Let me rephrase it so there's no confusion. My colleague points out it could be confusing. Is it an actual crime -- sorry. Is an actual crime such as shelling of the Old Town punishable immaterial of it being peacetime or state of war or imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As -- may I rephrase it then in the command light.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a commander, would you view as an actual crime the shelling of the Old Town as an actual crime being punishable immaterial of it being peacetime or state of war or imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would consider it to be a punishable crime irrespective of the state that the country is in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you consider, as a commander, the fact that a declaration of war had not been made as an impediment in any way to investigating the shelling of the Old Town in October, November, and December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should not be an impediment. I would always consider it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the 2nd Operational Group in command of all the units - JNA, TO, volunteers - all units involved in the Dubrovnik operations from 1st of October, 1991, until May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At all times during the period 1 October through 31 December 1991, were all of the battalions of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, in particular the 3rd and 4th Battalions, within the overall composition of the 2nd Operational Group even when they were under the direct subordination of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were always under the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that the 472nd Motorised Brigade was the unit that faced the most serious problems, especially in terms of its shortage of trained personnel in the use of artillery. You also stated that since you did not consider there to be a serious threat to the 2nd Operational Group forces from the Croatian forces in the region, you did not consider it necessary to have the presence of heavy weapons so close to the city of Dubrovnik, including the Old Town. Under these circumstances in this context, what would you have considered to be appropriate weapons to have been deployed in the area, especially considering the proposal which you made to General Strugar to withdraw the brigade, the 472nd Brigade, from the area? What alternative could you have suggested?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that it was sufficient, in close touch with the Dubrovnik Defence forces, to have a unit - the Mixed Detachment of the Territorial Defence was an appropriate unit - which could have carried out that task. That is what I thought. And ultimately, if that was not possible, it could be a battalion but with an artillery that was far away, at a distance from which it could not target the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain why General Strugar, who was aware of the clear risks that the scenario of the battalion entailed, kept the untrained reservists equipped with artillery and mortars, deployed within firing range of the Old Town, given that you had advised against it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in no way does this come from the cross-examination. This is a continuation of the examination-in-chief. I do not recall any such thing from the cross-examination. All of these subjects were dealt with in detail in the examination-in-chief. If there is any section of the cross-examination where this was referred to, may she please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got your message. Can you assist us, Ms. Somers, as to how this arises in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This has been repeated during the course of cross-examination, but in the interests of time, I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you do, we will receive now the Official Gazette of the 18th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we could ask, please, P120 -- Exhibit P120, tab 20; P124, tab 22A; and P132, tab 30. They are three maps we've just asked to have presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: While the maps are being presented or getting ready, I'd like to ask you, the various maps that were tendered into evidence through your testimony, you indicated that there are some inaccuracies. Are -- I'm going to ask you if you can very quickly go through some of them and just indicate whether or not they played any particular relevance.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the maps are faithful to the original, and if there are some imprecisions, they do not affect the content and the substance of what these maps depict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to confirm what you've just said, Admiral, do you need to see the maps? Because if you don't, if you're able to stand by what you've just said without showing us anything in particular, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have no objections. I think that it's those maps. At least, this one is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you identified JNA positions on the maps --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Usher, they don't need to be shown to the witness now. He's answered a general question. Thank you and the court officer for your work in getting them out so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you identified the JNA positions on the maps, Admiral, did you use the positions indicated on those maps as your point of reference or do you have personal knowledge of the positions within the relevant time frames, and is that how you're able to identify the positions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know the positions, and I know the terrain of the areas that the units were deployed in, and everything that is shown on these maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And these were two 2nd Operational Group positions that we were referring to, Admiral. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Admiral, with respect to your visit to the 2nd Operational Group command post on the 5th of December after the negotiations in Cavtat and thereafter the visit to your forward command post in Kupari, it was your position that when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2002, you had no recollection of it. In cross-examination, you testified in reference to your discussion with General Strugar concerning the negotiations, that General Strugar indicated to you that the issue of the checking of ships at the port of Gruz should not be his concern but a naval concern and that the agreement should proceed. Now, the question is: Was the issue of checking ships at the Gruz port discussed between you and General Strugar when you met him at his command post on the 5th of December after the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. We all remember that the witness said that he did not remember his day in Trebinje. He said that he reconstructed it on the basis of what others -- actually, that's what he said during the cross-examination when the difference was shown to him, the discrepancy between the interview and the examination-in-chief. He said, "I don't remember" or Kozaric or whoever told him. But this is not his own recollection. He said, "I do not know whether I was there. That's what others told me." And this is not contained in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question I see to be proper that was put, whether the issue of checking ships was discussed with General Strugar on the 5th of December. Are you able to answer that, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That precisely is the case. I failed to remember during the first interview whether I'd been there or not, and so on. However, when asked later on, and also during the cross-examination, I said that I remembered precisely that and that only, that General Strugar, when we talked about checking ships, whether it would take place in the port of Gruz, inside the port or out at sea, that refreshed my memory and reminded me that I had discussed the individual items of the peace agreement with him. That means that I was with him there at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: With regard, Admiral, to the second call which you made to General Strugar from Cavtat -- excuse me. On the 6th of December, with regard to the second call that you made to General Strugar from Cavtat, you stated that you recall it with great clarity. What was discussed in the course of this second phone conversation, please? Briefly, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, among other things, what I told to the people of Dubrovnik and what I was about to say, whether I had been able to ascertain whether the Old Town was being targeted or not. That's what was discussed. I said that I would express my regret that this ever happened, and that my impression was that indeed there were shells falling on the Old Town. He said roughly as follows: That we should not express our apologies to anyone. It was probably their mistake, it was probably their fault, and they were to blame for these operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard, Admiral, to the role played by the General Staff in the Dubrovnik operation, was it the case that the General Staff provided the general objectives at the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At which command level were combat orders as well as operational and tactical objectives issued? For example, decisions as to where to deploy units or unit subordination, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the level of the operational and strategic command such as the 2nd Operational Group. That was the level at which units were deployed, at which decisions were made in which area units would be active and what their tasks would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I please ask the ushers to show Defence D46. Is it inconvenient to ask you also to show -- to juxtapose P102. It might make it easier for the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have two exhibits which will be presented, and I can begin to ask you the question. At the request of Defence counsel -- at the request of Defence counsel, you prepared Exhibit D46, Admiral. Do you see it, D46, indicating all the units subordinated under the 9th VPS as of the 6th of December. Can you explain, please, the difference between Exhibit P102 and D46. Do you see them? Do you have them both in front of you, Admiral? I think you -- I think you have one exhibit that is incorrectly given.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tab 4, P102. Tab 4, P102. It's the first chart, the first -- the -- yes, that's it. If I've given you the wrong exhibit, I beg your pardon. Tab 4, P120. If I given you the -- 102, tab 4. It's our mistake. I'm sorry, it was copied incorrectly. It's P100. A million apologies. P100, tab 2. I'm so sorry to all of you. Looking at these two charts, Admiral, do you recognise -- look at them. Yes? Can you explain the difference between D46 that was prepared at the request of the Defence and P102 -- P100. I'm sorry, I'm doing it again.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document - I'm not sure what the number is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, please. Why are more units indicated in one, in D46, than in the other document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document that's displayed on the ELMO, we have indications pursuant to a request of the Defence. I gave all the formation units of the 9th VPS Military Naval Sector in peacetime, all the units that are part of the Military Naval Sector establishment-wise regardless of their active involvement or non-involvement in the Dubrovnik operation. And up here, in this other document, you have units under the 9th VPS that were temporarily resubordinated to me for purposes of the Dubrovnik operation. So establishment-wise, these are not my units, these were merely temporarily resubordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, did the units which the Defence asked you to add to your chart D46, did they play any combat role of significance during the time period relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had three units; 16th Border Naval Detachment -- 16th Border Naval Detachment, next the 107th or, rather, 140th Mobile Coastal Division - this unit was re-established - and then from the TOC, these three artillery pieces that were temporarily resubordinated to the sector. Only those three units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, moving on. You testified as to the temporary subordination of units being a factor which contributed to instability among the troops. Among the troops. Now, these temporary subordinations, who ordered the changes that resulted in these temporary subordinations of units, and in whose competence was it to decide the temporary or permanent status of such subordinations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the competence of my superior command, the command of the 2nd Operational Group, they're the ones who ordered this, these resubordinations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, returning for just one second, I think -- I looked back on the record and my question to you about those additional units on the chart that the Defence asked you to fill out, to add to, the units that the Defence asked about, did they play any significant combat role during the Dubrovnik operation? Just a yes or no would be helpful. You can focus it even to the 6th of December, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no significant role.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: P45, tab 14, please. I'm going to ask you a question, and I hope we can move through it quickly. The -- this is the three up, three down order. Do you recognise it, of General Adzic? The order is addressed to commands at the military district levels and the operational group levels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
